# Retrieval-Augmented Generation {#sec-rag}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements use 3,397 real Turkish news
articles — the XL-Sum test split @sec-summarization worked on — because
chunking is only interesting on documents that have internal structure.
@sec-rag-longcontext's needle test uses invented facts, so a correct answer
is very unlikely to come from the model's prior knowledge, and scoring is by
exact match. Retrieval mechanics belong to @sec-retrieval and are cited
rather than repeated. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `qwen3.5:9b`,
`snowballstemmer` 3.1.1, NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5. The model's full digest, the context-window
setting, the full prompt template, how the 40 facts were generated and the
item-level answers were not recorded; checking the tables independently would
need them published.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- compare the token cost of a long context with a short selected one on a
  simple needle test, and say which of the usual reasons was tested here and
  which tasks the result does not generalise to [@lewis2020rag; @liu2024lost];
- design the canonical pipeline and name what each stage is responsible for;
- choose a chunk size deliberately, knowing what it trades;
- attribute a wrong answer to the stage that caused it, before tuning
  anything.

## Why not just paste everything into the prompt? {#sec-rag-longcontext}

First, what the name means. **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** is the
general name for systems that fetch relevant content to support generation
with external knowledge. Its most common form is a simple recipe: when a question arrives, *search* your own documents for the few
passages most likely to contain the answer, *paste* those passages into the
prompt, and *ask* the model to answer from them. The search is @sec-retrieval's
subject; this chapter is about everything around it. The original formulation
[@lewis2020rag] trained the retriever and the generator together. This chapter
covers the common two-stage implementation that keeps them separate, indexing
documents in advance and handing selected passages to the generator at query
time; variants with query rewriting, multiple retrievals or retrieval during
generation also exist.

RAG exists because [models are frozen and your knowledge is not]{.hl}. That
is the permanent reason, and three related reasons stand beside it. **Private
data:** your organisation's documents and long-tail facts the model rarely saw
in training are absent from its parameters or weakly represented. **Citation:**
each retrieved chunk can carry a source id, which makes the answer checkable —
but whether the cited source actually supports the claim has to be checked
separately. **Less hallucination:** retrieving the right evidence can reduce
hallucination by helping the model build its answer from the text in front of
it rather than from memory — something to measure in your own system — but it
does not eliminate it: retrieval can fetch the wrong chunk, the model can
ignore what arrived, and the chunk itself can be wrong; @sec-rag-failures
separates these cases. But context windows kept growing, and every time
they did, somebody argued the problem had gone away: if the whole corpus fits,
why retrieve?

There are three common answers — **cost**, because every input token is
processed on every request, and most services bill for it; **access control**, because a prompt cannot
enforce who may see which document; and **recency**, because a cached prompt
goes stale. All three hold depending on the application, with one qualification worth making now: the
second and third are things retrieval *lets you build*, not properties the
label confers. A retrieval layer gives you a place to filter by permission and
a place to re-index. But an index that does not filter out documents a user may
not read still leaks them, just through one more step, and an index nobody refreshes is
as stale as the prompt it replaced. The fourth answer, also often repeated, is
that **a model does not use a long context evenly**.

All four can be measured: token and latency cost with prices and timing,
permission boundaries with access tests, recency with index freshness, and
context use with the model's behaviour. Each needs its own test under the
chosen system's conditions. The first three depend on your infrastructure, the
fourth on the model; this chapter measured the fourth with a simple needle test.
On the model and task used, [I saw no position-dependent drop]{.hl}; the result
does not generalise to harder evidence-finding tasks.

### The needle test

The design has to leave no room for a generous grader, so it is deliberately
crude. Take one invented fact — *the approved 2025 budget for project ZRG-14 is
743,912 lira* — whose invented project id and amount make a correct answer from
the model's prior knowledge very unlikely. Put it in a context alongside
genuine Turkish news articles as distractors. Ask for the number, and score by
exact match (which normalisation of number format and punctuation was applied,
and which forms were accepted, was not recorded for this run; write them down
in your own test). Then vary two things: how many
documents are in the context, and **where the fact sits**. There is no
retrieval step in this test — the documents go straight into the context — so
the `retrieval failures` counter in the last line does not measure retrieval
here.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 40 invented facts per cell, temperature 0, exact-match scoring

 documents  position  accuracy  prompt tokens
         1     start    100.0%            113
         5     start    100.0%            951
         5    middle    100.0%            953
         5       end    100.0%            949
        10     start    100.0%          2,005
        10    middle    100.0%          2,007
        10       end    100.0%          1,987
        20     start    100.0%          4,106
        20    middle    100.0%          4,115
        20       end    100.0%          4,112
        40     start    100.0%          8,318
        40    middle    100.0%          8,313
        40       end    100.0%          8,316
        80     start    100.0%         16,744
        80    middle    100.0%         16,720
        80       end    100.0%         16,775

16 conditions, 640 queries, 0 retrieval failures, 0 errors
```

**No drop is visible.** Not a gradient, not a dip in the middle, not a wobble
at 80 documents and 16,775 tokens: each of the 16 conditions scored 40/40. That
shows no large drop on this easy key-matching task; smaller positional effects
and failures on other tasks need their own tests.

### What a null result is worth

The temptation is to conclude that lost-in-the-middle is a myth. That
conclusion is not available from this table, and understanding why is more
useful than the table itself.

[A test every condition passes has little power to discriminate.]{.hl} What I
built is a very easy version of the task: one verbatim string, a distinctive
key (`ZRG-14`), a numeric answer, and a question that repeats the key exactly.
Because the question and the evidence share the same rare key, a perfect score
in every condition says something only about this easy matching; it does not
discriminate harder evidence-finding behaviour.

Other work shows the same limit. @modarressi2025nolima removed the literal lexical overlap between the
question and the needle and measured what happens: of thirteen models claiming
128K support, eleven fell below half their short-context baseline at 32K, and
GPT-4o dropped from 99.3% to 69.7%. A needle you can match on a token is a
different task from a needle you have to infer, and `ZRG-14` is about as
matchable as a needle gets. Language, models, metric and fact design all
change at once, so these results are not a direct comparison with this run;
they show the limit of the easy needle test.

Be careful with @liu2024lost too, in the other direction. That paper contains
*two* experiments, and only one is multi-document question answering. The other
is key–value retrieval over UUIDs — a pure string lookup with no semantic cue
at all, which is structurally similar to my test — and there the U-shape appeared
for some models and not for others. So a flat result on one 9B model is not a
contradiction of that paper; it is consistent with the model-to-model
variation the paper reports. What the multi-document half adds is the harder condition, where the
relevant passage must be identified on meaning rather than matched on a rare
token, and that is where the effect is most robust.

Context length alone does not seem to explain the difference either: their
multi-document setting tops out at 30 passages of at most 100 tokens each,
about 4,400–5,200 tokens on average depending on the tokenizer, roughly between
a quarter and a third of my longest condition. The lengths were counted with
different tokenizers and prompt formats, so this is only an approximate
comparison of magnitude. The difficulty of the needle is a plausible
explanation, not the only one. Their measurements were also taken on a 2023
generation of models, and long-context handling is precisely the thing that has
had the most engineering attention since.

One caveat the table cannot show. With 40 queries per cell, a perfect score has
a 95% Wilson lower bound of **91.2%**. That is a single cell's interval, not a
test of the difference between positions: testing a positional difference
needs paired results for the same facts at different positions and a threshold
fixed in advance (whether the same 40 facts were reused across positions was
not recorded). Read roughly, this design can rule out a drop the
size of the one @liu2024lost reported for GPT-3.5-Turbo in the multi-document
setting (about twenty points, from 75.8% with the answer first to 53.8% with it
in the middle of twenty documents), and cannot rule out an eight-point one. This run showed no large drop; it does
not rule out a small one. The claim is "no *large* positional effect", not "no positional
effect".

So the honest statement of what I measured is narrow, and I would rather write
the narrow true thing than the wide familiar one: **on this model, at up to
16,775 tokens, with a lexically easy needle, no positional effect large enough
for forty queries per cell to see.**

If your retrieval task looks like that, on a similar-sized model at similar
context lengths, position is probably not your first worry. If it
does not, this table tells you nothing about your case — and the way to find
out is to run the same experiment with *your* needles, at different evidence
positions and lengths; plan the sample size around the difference you want to
detect.

### The argument that survives

Look at the token column instead of the accuracy column, because that is where
the measurement actually lands.

```text
  1 document      113 prompt tokens    100.0%
 80 documents  16,775 prompt tokens    100.0%

                148x the input, for identical accuracy
```

[In this test the cost of not retrieving is not a wrong answer; it is about
148 times the input tokens for the same accuracy.]{.hl} The 80-document prompt
held 16,775 input tokens, the one-document prompt 113, and the measured
accuracy was the same. That ratio is not directly a price or latency ratio;
both depend on the provider, caching, output length and the cost of retrieval,
and have to be worked out separately. The input is processed again on every
request that cannot be served from a cache, and as the context grows,
attention's quadratic share of the compute grows with it, but end-to-end
latency has to be measured separately. (At this model size and around 16K tokens, most prefill compute is
still in layers that scale linearly; the quadratic term dominates at longer
contexts.)

**Prompt caching is the honest rebuttal to that number and it deserves stating
plainly.** A stable corpus prefix can be cached: cached input is billed at a
fraction of the fresh price — the rate, the cost of writing the cache and the
minimum prefix length vary by provider — and the prefill is skipped. A
hypothetical example: if the whole unchanging long prompt can be read from the
cache at a tenth of the fresh price, the roughly 148× ratio for input cost
alone falls to about 15× (16,775 / 10 / 113 ≈ 14.8). That sum leaves out cache
writes, a changing prefix, output and retrieval costs; the ratio is smaller,
still not free, and available only
while the prefix does not change, which is exactly the case retrieval exists
for. Note also that the 113-token baseline assumes *perfect* retrieval of
exactly one document; a real system passes $k$ chunks and pays to build and
query an index. The structural arguments below are the ones caching does not
touch.

That reframes the whole chapter. Retrieval is not a workaround for a model that
cannot read long inputs — on this easy test, this one read them without
trouble. Retrieval is [how you select a few chunks relevant to the question
instead of adding a whole large corpus to every request]{.hl}; the gain is
measured together with the number of chunks selected and the cost of
retrieval. It is also the natural place to
handle three things a single, shared, stuffed prompt handles badly: a corpus far
larger than any context window (most real document collections are gigabytes,
not thousands of tokens), knowledge that changes after training, and knowledge
that a given user is not allowed to see.

**What we will look at.** First the pipeline, which is worth naming stage by
stage only because each stage fails on its own and produces the same symptom,
together with the prompt that turns retrieved chunks into a grounded answer
with citations. Then chunking, which is the chapter's real experiment: eleven ways of cutting
the same corpus, queried two ways, where the best configuration under one kind
of question is the worst under the other and the received default is a guess
about questions its author never saw. Then the three failure modes and the
short piece of code that tells them apart — which is the thing you will reach for
every week, and the thing almost nobody builds before they need it — and the
standard metrics for scoring each half of the system.

## The canonical pipeline {#sec-rag-pipeline}

If retrieval is how you select a few chunks relevant to the question, the
next question is what the machinery actually consists of. A typical RAG system
has seven stages (some, such as reranking, are not present in every system). Naming them separately is what makes @sec-rag-failures
possible, because each one can fail on its own.

::: {.fig-cap}
The upper row is built once; the lower row runs on every request. The three
failure modes along the bottom — one at retrieval, two at generation — all
produce the *same* symptom, a wrong answer, which is why @sec-rag-failures is
about telling them apart before tuning anything. Coverage of the required
evidence passed to the generator bounds answers grounded in that evidence; that
bound equals recall@k numerically only with complete relevance judgements and
a single required piece of evidence. Parsing and chunking errors can also
happen before retrieval.
:::
::::

Stages 3 to 6 — embedding, the index (exhaustive, or an approximate
nearest-neighbour index, *ANN*, that trades a little recall for speed), top-*k*
retrieval and cross-encoder reranking — were @sec-retrieval's subject, and this
chapter treats them as given. Two things about the diagram are worth saying out
loud, because both are routinely skipped.

::: {.column-margin}
The pipeline is also the thing every RAG survey enumerates — @gao2023rag is
the most complete map of the variants, and worth skimming once you have built
one yourself, so the taxonomy attaches to something. Note that the whole
diagram assumes retrieval happens exactly once, before generation. Systems
that decide *whether* and *when* to retrieve, and critique what came back —
Self-RAG [@asai2024selfrag] is the reference design — are @sec-agentic-rag's
subject, and they only make sense once this fixed pipeline is working and
measured.
:::

**Stage 1 failures are easy to miss.** A PDF table can become a column of
disconnected numbers; a two-column layout can interleave; a scanned page may
produce no text at all without OCR. No amount of embedding quality recovers text
that was destroyed on the way in, and the failure is invisible downstream —
the pipeline runs, the numbers look plausible, and the answer is wrong for a
reason nobody is looking at. Read the parsed output of a chosen sample of
documents by hand before tuning anything else.

**Stage 5 sets a bound on stage 7.** What to measure is how often the chunks
passed to the generator carry the required evidence (*evidence coverage*). For
questions that need a single, completely marked piece of evidence, 80%
evidence coverage means at most an 80% chance of an answer grounded in *the
retrieved text*; no prompt engineering reaches the other 20%. (The model may
still answer some of them from its own memory, but those answers are not
grounded in anything you retrieved.) A document-level hit is not the same
rate: the document may arrive while the needed passage sits in another chunk,
and the same fact may appear in another document — @sec-retrieval separates
these conditions.

::: {.column-margin}
Which is why the two halves of a RAG system want different metrics and
different people looking at them. The retrieval half is judged on not missing;
the generation half on using what arrived and refusing when it did not.
@sec-rag-failures is about telling those two apart, and it is harder than it
sounds because both produce the same symptom: a wrong answer.
:::

### Stage 7: a grounded prompt, with citations

The generate stage is usually a single prompt, and its *shape* matters more
than its wording. The goal is a **grounded** answer: one in which every claim
can be traced to the retrieved text rather than to the model's own memory.
Three habits get you most of the way.

- **Number the chunks and ask for citations.** Give each chunk an ID, its
  source and the document version, ask the model to mark each factual claim
  with the ID of the chunk that supports it, and then check claim–source
  agreement separately. A citation does not guarantee support, but it turns
  "trust me" into something a reader, or a script, can check: does chunk [2]
  actually say that?
- **Give the model a legal way out.** State exactly what to write when the
  chunks do not contain the answer. @sec-rag-failures explains why a system
  without this option never abstains.
- **Documents first, question last — as a starting layout.** Some model
  providers recommend putting long material at the top and the instruction and
  question at the end; that advice is specific to the model and API. Placing
  the highest-ranked chunks at the start of the block is a useful starting
  point, but because this chapter's needle test detected no position effect,
  its benefit was not measured here; test where the document block and the
  question go on the model you use.

```text
Answer the question using ONLY the numbered documents below.
After each sentence, cite the document that supports it, e.g. [2].
If the documents do not contain the answer, reply exactly:
"The documents do not answer this question."

[1] (source: budget-2025.pdf, page 14)
The approved 2025 budget for project ZRG-14 is 743,912 lira. ...

[2] (source: board-minutes-2025-03.docx)
...

Question: What is the approved 2025 budget for project ZRG-14?
```

A citation is itself a claim, and models do cite chunk [2] for a sentence that
chunk 2 does not support. So check citations rather than display them: for each
cited sentence, ask whether the cited chunk supports it, and count the
failures. Use number and name matching as a first check — it can also approve
a wrong relation —, and examine claims involving relations and inference with
a method validated on a human-labelled sample (a judge model has an error rate
too).
That count is the *faithfulness* score defined at the end of @sec-rag-failures.

Retrieved text carries one more risk specific to RAG: chunks hold the words of
whoever wrote the document, not yours. An instruction placed inside them
("ignore previous instructions and ...") enters the same text field as your
instruction and can affect the model's behaviour, so treat retrieved text as
untrusted data and never carry out the commands in it as instructions. This is
called indirect prompt injection and is @sec-agent-security's subject; the risk
grows as your corpus takes in outside content.

Two security details belong in the pipeline too. Permission is granted per
document but retrieval happens per chunk: every chunk should carry its source
document's access list as metadata, the filter should apply before chunks
enter the prompt, and the chunks should be relabelled when the document's
permissions change. Do not rely only on the metadata from indexing time:
check permission at query time against the document's current permissions.
Citations should also be tied to the document's *version* (document id plus
version or content hash): if the document is later updated, the chunk [2]
that an old answer cited may no longer contain that sentence.

## Chunking is a modelling decision {#sec-rag-chunking}

Stage 2 is the one this chapter measures. A chunk is the unit you retrieve;
chunk size decides both **what is retrievable at all** and how much context
reaches the generator. So it is a decision, not a preprocessing detail — and
it moves two things in opposite directions at once:

- Smaller chunks can be *more narrowly focused* on the query. A 50-word chunk
  that matches the query is often largely about the query.
- Smaller chunks mean *more of them*; that can split context, grows the index
  and the number of candidates, and leaves each chunk less context to
  disambiguate itself.

Common defaults suggest a number — 512 tokens, 200 words, "about a
paragraph". The balance is worth measuring on your own documents and queries,
because the
trade above depends on how long your documents are and how localised the
answers are within them.

### The experiment

The retriever is held fixed so that only the cutting changes. 3,397 Turkish
news articles, indexed eleven different ways with the same BM25 retriever, and
queried under **two kinds of question** — because a single kind would have
shown only one side of chunk size. Both kinds are proxies derived from the
target document: they do not represent a real user query mix, and the results
show how the chunking strategies behave on these two proxy tasks; real
question-answering success has to be measured separately.

- **A. article-level.** The query is the article's professional one-sentence
  summary. *What is this document about?*
- **B. fact-level.** The query is six content words drawn from **one sentence**
  of the article. Each word is then replaced by another inflected form of the
  same stem (as in *seçim* → *seçimde*), so the query does not repeat the text's
  exact word forms. *Where is this specific detail?*

A hit means any chunk of the source article. Read that definition against each
condition before reading the numbers. In condition A it is the right target —
the question *is* the article. In condition B it is a proxy and a generous one:
retrieving the correct article's *other* paragraph counts as a success even
though the sentence the query was drawn from is not in the returned chunk, so
condition B's numbers bound article-level retrieval rather than measuring
fact-level evidence. Getting the stricter number needs supporting-span
annotation — record which sentence each query came from and require the chunk
to contain it — which this run does not have. So below, both conditions'
measure is called *source-article hit@k*; condition B's numbers are not
fact-level recall. Build times are not reported: an
earlier run's timings were contaminated by a concurrent job on the same
machine, and a number I cannot stand behind does not belong in a table.

```text

fixed 50w, no overlap       24,266     51   57.0%   81.8%   67.1    96.5%   99.8%   97.8
fixed 100w, no overlap      12,390     99   66.5%   86.5%   75.2    95.5%   98.2%   96.7
fixed 200w, no overlap       6,459    187   70.0%   88.5%   78.3    94.0%   97.2%   95.4
fixed 400w, no overlap       4,074    297   72.5%   90.2%   80.1    93.8%   97.8%   95.6
fixed 100w, overlap 25      15,983     98   65.8%   87.0%   74.4    97.5%   99.8%   98.6
fixed 100w, overlap 50      21,890    101   66.0%   84.8%   73.7    97.2%   99.8%   98.5
fixed 200w, overlap 50       8,070    184   71.5%   88.0%   78.8    97.0%   99.8%   98.3

```

The columns: `chunks` is the number of chunks in the index, `w/chk` the mean
words per chunk; `R@1` and `R@5` are the share of queries for which any chunk
of the source article is in the top 1 or top 5 (source-article hit@1 and @5 —
not standard passage recall computed with complete relevance judgements); and
`MRR` is the mean reciprocal rank of the source article's first chunk, out of
100. In the rows, `fixed` is a fixed-size window, `overlap` the number of
overlapping words, and `sentence-aligned` chunks aligned to sentence
boundaries.

### What it says

The main observation, briefly: in these two proxy conditions, the 400-word
window that gave the highest source-article hit@1 in A gave the lowest in B.
The numbers and the slope chart follow; but first, four things bound this
table before any of it can be read, and all four are properties of the design
rather than of chunking.

**The sweep is narrower than eleven rows suggest.** The mean article is 366
words, so a 400-word window leaves most articles intact — 4,074 chunks from
3,397 articles — and `fixed 400w` is close to a noisy copy of `whole article`.
The range actually swept is 50 to 200 words.

**Rank is not a fair axis when the units differ in size.** At rank 1 the
whole-article index hands the generator 366 words and the 50-word index hands
it 51, so part of condition A's ordering is simply *more text wins*. The
comparison the table is missing is hit rate at an equal word budget — roughly
whole article at $k{=}1$ against 200w at $k{=}2$, 100w at $k{=}4$, 50w at
$k{=}7$. In condition B the 50-word index beats the 400-word one at rank 1 with
about a *sixth* of the text; whether the gap would grow at an equal budget was
not measured. Mean word counts are only an approximate start: actual chunk
lengths, metadata, repetition and question tokens vary. The real comparison
equalises the token budget actually passed to the generator and measures
evidence-sentence coverage.

**Recall@5 is not deduplicated by article.** Five chunks from a 50-word index
can be five slices of one document; five chunks from the whole-article index
are necessarily five different documents. Fine-grained indexes are therefore
penalised at rank 5 because several of their five slots can go to slices of
the same article, and an unknown part of the
ten-point R@5 gap in condition A is that artefact rather than chunking.

**And $n = 400$ per condition, so a 95% interval is about ±4.6 points in A and
±1.9 in B.** Do not turn that into "smaller differences are indistinguishable",
which is the error this book keeps warning about: those are intervals on single
proportions, and the systems here are compared on the *same* 400 queries. A
paired test conditions on the queries the two systems disagree about and can
resolve gaps far inside an unpaired interval. The queries are shared across all
eleven systems, so had the per-query results been kept, a paired difference
and interval for the binary hit (McNemar, for instance) could be computed; MRR
needs paired resampling, and picking the best of eleven rows has a
multiple-comparison effect that must be accounted for too. This run did not
record per-query results; we report the unpaired numbers, which is the weaker
choice, and the intervals above should be read as a caution against
over-reading small gaps rather than as a test that settles them.

With those in hand: [in these two proxy conditions, the chunk size with the
highest value in one gave the lowest in the other.]{.hl} Chunks at or above article length lead condition A — 400-word
chunks at 72.5% and whole articles at 71.8%, indistinguishable from each other —
and fall to the bottom of condition B: 400-word chunks are last at **93.8%**,
whole articles eighth of eleven at 96.0%. Fifty-word chunks are last in A at
**57.0%** and mid-table in B at **96.5%**, above both. The 15.5-point gap in A
is far outside any interval above. The reversal in B is smaller — 2.7 points
between 50-word and 400-word chunks, 4.0 between the best and the worst — and
sits at the edge of what unpaired intervals can resolve, which is exactly where
the paired test would earn its keep. Their rank correlation is negative
(Spearman $\rho \approx -0.62$), so they come close to opposite orderings of the
same eleven systems. That is a fact about ranks, not a decision-level
difference: condition B's differences sit within a 4.0-point total range, and
without paired item-level results small rank differences should not be counted
as reliable superiority.

Ranked side by side, the two columns' orders diverge clearly:

line is 400-word chunks going from first to last; the green one is

condition B's numbers are not evidence-sentence hits. Read the numbers as well
as the positions: condition B's whole spread is four points against condition

::::

The working hypothesis from this experiment: **choose chunk size for the
granularity the questions need, and test it on your own queries.**

Ask what a document
is about and a chunk that holds only part of it can only match part of your
query, so bigger wins. Ask where a specific fact is and a short chunk that
contains it is largely *about* it, so smaller can pull ahead — a plausible
explanation is BM25's length normalisation seen from two sides; this
experiment did not test the mechanism separately.

Two more results in that table were not obvious to me before running it.

**In this experiment, overlap came with a gain only in condition B.** At 100 words, adding a 25-word
overlap moved condition B from 95.5% to **97.5%** — 18 errors in 400 down to
10, a *net* movement of eight queries. (How many queries changed in each
direction is what the paired test above needs, and this run did not record it.)
The same overlap moved condition A from 66.5% to 65.8%, three queries and well
inside that condition's noise band. A small difference is not the same as a
demonstrated absence of one, so decide in advance how large a change would
matter to you and read the result against that.

A plausible explanation: overlap helps when a fact can straddle a chunk
boundary, and not when the query describes the whole document. But whether
overlap actually brings the evidence passage, and how reliable these
differences are, still has to be tested; on other tasks overlap may help. So
treat overlap as an option to measure rather than a general-purpose safety
margin: if you see no gain on your own questions, you are paying for 29% more
chunks (a 25-word overlap at 100 words: 15,983 against 12,390 chunks).

**Sentence-aligned chunks scored highest in B — with one confound named.** Sentence-aligned
chunks of about 100 words scored **97.8%** in condition B against fixed 100-word
windows' 95.5%, and did it with *fewer* chunks than the overlapping variant that
came second (14,500 against 15,983). One caveat before crediting all of that to
structure: the sentence-aligned index averages **86** words per chunk against
the fixed index's **99**, and condition B already rewards smaller chunks.
Interpolating the fixed-size series linearly, an 86-word *fixed* window would
land somewhere near 95.8%; but that assumes a linear curve and does not give a
causal share of the 2.3 points to structure. Separating structure from size
needs a length-matched control — `fixed 86w, no overlap` is the missing row in
that table. What survives in this experiment is that keeping sentences whole
added no chunk cost, scored higher than the fixed split, and reached the level
of the overlapping variant with fewer chunks (97.8% against 97.5% is a single
query out of 400).

::: {.column-margin}
Note what the R@5 columns do. In condition B, every configuration is between
97.2% and 100% at rank 5, so if your generator reads five chunks, the B half of
this table is close to a rounding error — for finding the right *article*,
which is all these columns measure. Condition A is different: R@5 still spans
ten points (81.8% to 91.8%), so for questions about a whole document the choice
matters even at five chunks. Do not promote the flat B column into a claim
about the system either: whether the chunk that arrives actually carries the
answering sentence is a different question this run does not score. If your
generator reads one chunk, the R@1 columns are your system.
@sec-retrieval made the same point about fusion,
and it generalises: [the metric that matters is the one your consumer actually
reads.]{.hl}
:::

### Structural boundaries are a good start {#structure-beats-arithmetic}

Whatever size you land on, **use the document's structural boundaries as chunk
candidates**: sections, articles, clauses, speaker turns, table rows. Pack
sentences and table rows to the target length without splitting them where
possible, split very long sections separately, and test the choice with your
own queries and evidence labels — this experiment tested only news sentences. A boundary drawn at a
fixed word count lands mid-sentence, mid-clause, mid-argument, and produces
two chunks that are each locally plausible and jointly wrong — the failure
@sec-summarization found in map-reduce, arriving here through a different
door.

Overlap is the crude repair: repeat the last *n* words of each chunk at the
start of the next, so a fact that straddles a boundary appears whole in at
least one chunk — provided the fact is shorter than the overlap and does not
straddle two boundaries. A 25-word overlap does not *guarantee* that a claim
whose subject and qualifier are forty words apart lands whole in some chunk,
though at some offsets a 100-word window will hold both. That is why it is a
repair and not a guarantee.

It costs index size: a window of $w$ words advancing by $w - o$ words (overlap
$o$) produces about $w/(w-o)$ times as many chunks — 100/75 ≈ 1.33 for the
25-word overlap, 1.29 measured, since an article shorter than one window
yields one chunk either way; the approximate ratio holds for long documents.
The table above suggests that keeping the document's own boundaries can give a
similar result with fewer chunks: in B, sentence-aligned chunks reached 97.8%
source-article hit and fixed windows padded with overlap 97.5% — one query
apart, not evidence of superiority — and the sentence-aligned index was 9%
smaller. Whether evidence-sentence success was also the same was not
measured.

Two document types where fixed-size chunking simply fails:

- **Tables.** A row is often meaningless without its column headers. Before
  chunking, keep the row and column headers, units and any needed super-headers.
  If each row stands on its own, you can serialise it into text; if not, index
  the table as a structural unit and pass the relevant part to the generator
  together.
- **Anything with cross-references.** *As described in section 4* is
  meaningless once section 4 is a different chunk in a different part of the
  index. Either resolve the reference at ingestion or accept the loss and
  measure it.

### So what should you do?

**One boundary on all of this first: every number above is BM25.** The likely
mechanism behind condition B — short chunks pulling ahead because they are
largely about the query — has to do with BM25's length normalisation, so it may
be a property of the scorer as much as of the cutting. A dense retriever may
have no explicit length normalisation like BM25's `b`, but length still
matters: a maximum sequence length that truncates, a pooling step (often a mean
over tokens) that squeezes a long chunk into one vector, and the lengths the
model was trained on can all produce different behaviour. Do not assume either
the direction or the optimum without re-evaluating the same strategies with the
dense model you choose, and the pipeline diagram at the top of
this chapter shows an embedding stage, so a reader is entitled to assume
otherwise unless we say this.

Measure it, on your corpus, with your retriever, with queries shaped like the
ones you will get. But if you need a starting point before you have that:

- Chunk on **structure** — sentences, paragraphs, sections, clauses, rows — and
  pack to a target size rather than cutting at one.
- Measure size and overlap on your real queries together with evidence-chunk
  coverage, answer accuracy and cost. In this experiment's proxy conditions,
  fact queries did well at roughly 100–200 words and queries about what a
  document covers did well with larger chunks, up to whole documents; that
  range is not a general optimum.
- Treat **overlap** as a boundary repair to measure, not a default; in this
  experiment it came with a gain only on fact-shaped queries.
- If your questions are genuinely both kinds, consider indexing at two
  granularities rather than compromising at one. Measure first: on this corpus
  the best compromise (200 words, 50 overlap) was only about a point behind the
  best configuration in each condition; without paired results that gap cannot
  be resolved, and it is not guaranteed to be that small on yours.
- **Try retrieving small and generating big.** One method to try for the
  trade-off between targeting and context is *small-to-big* (or
  *parent-document*) retrieval: search small chunks in the index, but hand the
  generator the section around the matching chunk or the whole document;
  frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex have ready versions. It can raise
  token cost and distraction; compare the tokens sent, evidence coverage and
  answer quality against passing the small chunk directly. A sibling method
  prepends the document title, or a short context sentence placing the chunk
  in its document, to every chunk
  ([contextual retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)),
  so a chunk that is ambiguous on its own introduces itself. Neither was
  measured in this chapter.

## Failure modes, and attributing them {#sec-rag-failures}

A RAG system gives a wrong answer. Wrong answers usually show up at one of
three stages — retrieval, use of the retrieved evidence, or combining the
evidence — and each has a different fix; parsing, source and label faults need
checking separately too. So the first job is **not** to tune anything — it is
to locate the failure among these stages.

| failure | what happened | how you detect it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Retrieval miss** | the required evidence is not in the chunks passed to the generator (because of retrieval, chunking or parsing) | check whether the passed chunks hold evidence supporting the expected answer; if not, no grounded answer can be expected downstream |
| **Grounding miss** | the right chunk was returned and the model ignored it, or contradicted it | the chunk is in the context and the answer is not in the chunk |
| **Synthesis miss** | everything needed was there, spread across chunks, and the model combined it wrongly | all facts present, conclusion wrong |

: Three failures, one symptom {tbl-colwidths="[20,42,38]"}

The first step of the diagnostic can be built as a short loop:

```python
for q, expected in evaluation_set:
    hits = retrieve(q, k=10)                   # the same k the generator reads
    answer = generate(q, hits)
    if matches(answer, expected):
        continue                               # correct: nothing to attribute
    if not evidence_for(expected, hits):
        bucket["evidence missing"] += 1        # retrieval, chunking or parsing
    elif not claims_supported_by(answer, hits):
        bucket["grounding miss"] += 1          # inspect the prompt, or the model
    else:
        bucket["inspect: source, label or synthesis"] += 1   # look by hand
```

Read the three tests in order. Only wrong answers are attributed. If the
chunks passed to the generator hold no evidence for the expected answer —
because the document never arrived, the needed passage sat in another chunk,
or parsing lost it — nothing downstream could produce a grounded answer.
Checking the document id is not enough: the needed sentence may not be in the
returned chunk, and another document may carry the evidence. If the evidence
arrived but the generated claims are not supported by it, the model ignored or
contradicted its evidence. If every claim is supported and the conclusion is
still wrong, the last bucket collects three possible causes: the facts were
combined wrongly (synthesis), the retrieved document is wrong, stale or
contradicted by another document (a corpus error), or the reference answer is
wrong (a label error). Do not declare a synthesis error before checking the
document's currency and the reference's correctness; inspect this bucket by
hand. A supported but wrong answer drawn from a single chunk points at the
source rather than at synthesis. In practice `matches` is a normalised match or
a validated judge; `evidence_for` is an evidence label or a judge asking
whether evidence for the expected answer is in the passed chunks; and
`claims_supported_by` is the faithfulness check defined at the end of this
section.

[Do this before touching the embedding model.]{.hl} The default reflex when a
RAG system disappoints is to swap the embeddings, and the measurement in
@sec-retrieval's two synthetic conditions suggests it is not always the
biggest lever — the choice of
embedding model was worth 2.4 points on easy queries and 25.3 on hard ones,
while the choice between lexical and dense was worth *sixty to seventy*, in
whichever direction the query type dictated. And an embedding swap can only
fix the first of the three buckets.

### Two failures worth naming separately

Two of the ways a RAG system goes wrong sit awkwardly in that three-way table,
because both are consequences of choices you made rather than stages that
broke.

**Distraction.** On some tasks irrelevant retrieved context does not merely
fail to help; it can lower answer quality [@shi2023large]. That reframes *k* as
a trade rather than a "more is safer" dial: raising it improves evidence
coverage and imports noise, and on some tasks past some point the second
effect can win.

With the same caveat @sec-rag-longcontext earned, and it is worth being
explicit rather than quietly citing past it: **on my simple key-matching
test, putting 79 extra documents around the answer showed no drop.** Distraction
did not appear there either. @shi2023large's effect is measured on arithmetic
and reasoning problems, where an irrelevant clause can be *used* — pulled into
the chain of reasoning and acted on. Locating a string is not that kind of
task, and neither is most extraction. Evidence from RAG-style question
answering points the same way: in @liu2024lost's open-domain QA case study,
retriever recall kept rising as more documents were retrieved while the reader
model's accuracy saturated much earlier, with only 1–1.5 points gained beyond
20 documents.

So set the number of chunks on your own task by evidence coverage, answer
accuracy, latency and cost, and assume neither that the penalty exists nor
that it does not: **measure it before you budget for it**, which is what @sec-rag-exercises's fifth exercise asks you to
do.

**Refusal that never happens.** A system with no legal way to say *the
documents do not answer this* will usually answer anyway, from parametric
memory, fluently. (A model may sometimes say "I don't know" without an explicit
refusal string in the prompt, and giving it the option does not guarantee
abstention either.) @sec-prompting's rule applies exactly here: name the failure output,
make it easy to produce, and then check that the model actually uses it — on
questions you know the corpus cannot answer. That last test is often skipped, and it is the difference between a system that abstains and a system
that has never been given the option.

### Scoring the two halves

The three-way attribution works on single failures. To track a system over
time you want numbers, and the evaluation frameworks — RAGAS [@es2024ragas] and
its relatives — offer a common set that follows the same split. The names
recur in every tool and job interview, so here they are in plain terms:

| metric | half | the question it asks | score |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **context precision** | retrieval | are the retrieved chunks relevant, and are the relevant ones ranked near the top? | mean of precision@k at the ranks holding relevant chunks (Ragas has with-reference, without-reference, non-LLM and ID-based variants) |
| **context recall** | retrieval | does the retrieved text contain everything the reference answer needs? | share of the reference answer's claims found in the context |
| **faithfulness** | generation | is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved text? | supported claims ÷ all claims in the answer |
| **answer relevance** | generation | does the answer address the question that was asked? | in Ragas: the mean cosine similarity between the embeddings of the question and of questions an LLM generates from the answer (three by default) |

: Four common RAG metrics (Ragas names) {tbl-colwidths="[20,14,42,24]"}

These names are not single universal formulas: report the variant you use, the
reference fields it needs, its ranking computation and the judge model.

A worked example makes faithfulness concrete: an answer that makes four
claims, three of which the retrieved chunks support, scores 3/4 = 0.75, even
if the fourth claim happens to be true — faithfulness asks *where* a claim came
from, not whether it is correct. These metrics are signals of where a
failure may sit: low context recall suggests missing evidence, low faithfulness
suggests unsupported claims, and a wrong answer with both high points at a
synthesis, source or label error. But a low score can also come from a missing
reference, the claim-splitting step or a judge error; for a firm attribution,
inspect the chunk, source, reference label and judge decision by hand on a
sample.

Two cautions. First, a note on provenance: the RAGAS paper itself defines
faithfulness, answer relevance and *context relevance*; context precision and
context recall were added later in the library, and context recall needs a
reference answer written by a person. Second, every one of these numbers is produced by
an LLM judge that splits text into claims and checks each one, so its errors
are judge errors. @sec-summarization found two automatic faithfulness measures
that agreed on the ranking while flagging five summaries and eleven summaries
respectively, and overlapping on exactly one. Use the metrics for the
structure they impose, validate the judge on a sample you have labelled by hand
(@sec-llm-eval-judge shows how), and do not compare absolute scores across
tools.

## Intuition checks {#sec-rag-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Most of them are questions this chapter
settled with a measurement rather than an argument; where it did not, the
answer says so.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Context windows keep growing. Is RAG a temporary workaround?

No — and this chapter measured one cost item: on this needle test, answering
from 80 documents instead of the 1 that mattered used **about 148× the input
tokens for the same accuracy**. That is a token ratio; price and latency have
to be measured separately. The permanent reasons are different again: **the
model is frozen and your documents are not** — a retrieval step is how new,
private or changing information reaches a model that finished training before
it existed, and most real corpora are far larger than any context window
anyway. Access control is the other reason: a prompt cannot enforce who may
read which document, while retrieval gives you a point at which to select
current, permitted content — which still has to be implemented with correct
index updates and query-time permission checks. Long context and retrieval
are complements, not competitors — a bigger window changes how many chunks you
can afford to pass, not whether you needed to choose them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. What chunk size should you use?

It may depend on the granularity of your questions, and this chapter measured
how much the ranking moved in two synthetic query conditions: on the same
corpus, 400-word chunks led on article-level queries at **72.5%** source-article
hit@1 and came *last* on fact-level queries at **93.8%**, while 50-word chunks
did the reverse. Condition B only measures finding any chunk of the source
article, not the needed sentence. If you need a starting point before you have
measured, pack whole sentences to roughly 100–200 words and re-evaluate size
on your real questions by whether the supporting passage is found. If your
questions are genuinely of both kinds, consider indexing twice rather than
compromising once — and measure whether the compromise actually costs you
anything; on this corpus the gap was about a point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Should you add overlap between chunks?

Decide by measuring. Here, a 25-word overlap on 100-word chunks moved
source-article hit@1 on fact-level queries from 95.5% to **97.5%** and on
article-level queries from 66.5% to 65.8% — while adding 29% more chunks to the
index. The query-level reliability of those differences and overlap's effect
on real fact evidence were not measured; treat overlap as a repair to test for
facts that straddle a boundary, not a general safety margin. Chunking on
sentence boundaries also reached the level of overlapping fixed windows
(97.8% against 97.5%, one query apart) with a 9% smaller index.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your RAG system gives a wrong answer. What do you do first?

Attribute it, before tuning anything. First check whether the text passed to
the generator holds evidence supporting the expected answer — the wrong chunk
of the right article may have arrived, and another document may carry the
evidence. If not, inspect retrieval, chunking and parsing (a **retrieval
miss**); the prompt is irrelevant. If it does and the generated claims are not
supported by it, that is a **grounding miss**. If the claims are supported and
the conclusion is still wrong, assess the source, the label and a
**synthesis** error separately. One symptom, different fixes — and the default
reflex, swapping the embedding model, can only help with the first.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Is more retrieved context always safer?

No — but this is one of the answers the chapter did not measure for itself.
With a fixed ranking, taking more chunks does not reduce the coverage of
reachable candidates; but the length, order and noise of the context passed to
the generator can change answer quality. Irrelevant context can degrade answers
on some tasks [@shi2023large]; that evidence comes mostly from reasoning
problems (in RAG-style question answering, @liu2024lost shows accuracy
saturating early as more documents are retrieved). On this chapter's simple
needle test, putting 79 extra documents around the answer brought no drop. So
choose *k* by measuring evidence coverage, answer accuracy and cost on your own
task: every chunk you pass is processed on every request, so a *k* chosen by
superstition is a permanent line item.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your system never says "I don't know". Is that a prompting problem?

Often it is a *design* problem: if the system has no legal way to abstain, it
usually answers from parametric memory, fluently and without warning. Define an
explicit refusal output, make it cheap to produce, and then measure both the
unnecessary-refusal rate and the ungrounded-answer rate **on questions with and
without an answer**. Refusal behaviour depends on the prompt, the model and the
decision threshold; an explicit option alone is not enough, and systems without
one sometimes abstain too. @sec-decoding has the machinery for making the
abstention a real, thresholded decision.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-rag-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** Some of these are
adapted from topics in the two open interview sources introduced there, and
some are written around this chapter's RAG pipeline and experiments; none is
attributed to a particular company, and the numbers in the answers are this
chapter's own.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: Walk me through a RAG pipeline.**

Name the stages and say what each one can break, because a list of seven nouns
demonstrates nothing. Parse — where table rows and scanned pages can be lost,
silently. Chunk — which decides what is retrievable at all. Embed and index —
where an approximate index can quietly lower neighbour recall. Retrieve,
rerank, generate. Then give the relationship that matters: **coverage of the
required evidence passed to the generator bounds answers grounded in that
evidence**; it equals recall@k numerically only with complete relevance
judgements and a single required piece of evidence. So I track each stage
separately.

**Q: How do you choose a chunk size?**

By measuring it against the questions you expect, and the good answer names
*why* there is no universal number: chunk size trades targeting against
context, and which side wins depends on whether a question is about a whole
document or a specific fact. Cite the shape rather than a number — on one news
corpus, with BM25 and two synthetic query conditions, 400-word chunks gave the
highest source-article hit on article-level queries and the lowest on
fact-level ones. Then say how you would measure: compare a few chunk sizes that
keep structural boundaries on the same real queries, measuring supporting
evidence coverage, answer quality and token cost together; 100–200 words is
only one candidate to try.

**Q: Why does adding more retrieved context sometimes make answers worse?**

Because irrelevant context is not neutral — it can distract [@shi2023large] —
and because models do not always read a long context evenly [@liu2024lost]. Both are
reasons to treat *k* as a parameter tuned by measuring on your own task rather
than a safety margin. If you have run the needle test yourself, say what you found and
under what conditions, because the effect's size depends heavily on the model
and the task.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Your RAG system is wrong 30% of the time. How do you find out why?**

Refuse to guess, and attribute wrong answers in order: first check whether the
required evidence actually reached the generator, then whether the generated
claims are supported by it; for supported but wrong answers, inspect the
source, the reference label and synthesis separately, and check parsing and
permission-filter faults too. Say that you would run it *before* changing the
embedding model, because that is the reflex and it can help with the first
bucket at most. The follow-up worth volunteering is that this requires
logging the retrieved context alongside every answer — without it, failures
are unattributable after the fact.

**Q: How would you evaluate a RAG system?**

In two halves, because they fail independently: the retrieval half on recall@k
and nDCG against labelled queries, the generation half on faithfulness to the
retrieved context and on answer correctness. Frameworks like RAGAS
[@es2024ragas] follow this decomposition — context precision and recall,
faithfulness and answer relevance — and are worth using for the structure; but
I calibrate those automatic metrics on a human-labelled sample. Add the test
that is often skipped — questions the corpus cannot
answer, scored on whether the system abstains — and say plainly that automatic
faithfulness scores need validating before you trust them, which is
@sec-llm-eval's subject.

**Q: When would you not use RAG?**

When the knowledge is small and stable enough to sit in the prompt; when the
task needs the whole corpus rather than a few passages, such as "summarise
every complaint this quarter", where retrieval structurally cannot see enough;
and when the requirement is really a database query wearing a natural-language
costume. Where exact filtering and aggregation over structured records are
needed, an authorised, validated query layer (text-to-SQL over a schema, for
instance) is often more suitable; where the task needs evidence from
unstructured documents, retrieval and generation may suit better — and I test
both on real queries. Knowing where the technique stops is the part that separates a
practitioner from someone repeating an architecture diagram.

**Q: RAG or fine-tuning?**

Usually the wrong either-or. For facts that change, facts a user must be able
to check against a source and facts some users may not see, retrieval is
usually suitable: updating an index is often easier than retraining, answers
can cite their evidence, and permissions can be enforced per document — though
neither index updates nor permission checks are automatic or free. For format,
tone and a narrow task done reliably, fine-tuning can help; fine-tuning can
teach knowledge too, but adding facts reliably and removing them later is
hard, and RAG also shapes behaviour through the prompt and the selected
evidence. Decide by measuring cost, deletion, permissions and accuracy in the
application. The two can compose: a model fine-tuned on your format,
answering over retrieved documents that supply your facts. @sec-decision-tree
walks through the decision question by question.

## Lab: a RAG system that tells you which stage failed {#sec-rag-lab}

In this lab you build an evaluation harness that records failures at the
retrieval and generation stages of a RAG pipeline: given a wrong answer, it
names the stage that may be responsible.

### Step 1 — fifty questions, written before any code

Choose fifty answerable questions from your own corpus, if possible resembling
real user questions, and add at least twenty that the corpus **cannot**
answer; those are how you test abstention (with five, a single error moves the
rate by 20 points). For each, record the needed evidence and an answerability
label before seeing any model output, ideally by someone who did not build the
system. Do this first, because questions written after you have seen the
system's output drift towards questions the system can already answer.

### Step 2 — two chunkings, not one

Index the corpus twice: whole documents, and sentence-packed chunks of about
150 words. You now have the two ends of @sec-rag-chunking's trade on your own
data. Compare them on the same queries; record the token budget passed to the
generator, and score whether the supporting evidence is actually in the passed
chunks, separately from document hits.

### Step 3 — measure evidence coverage before generating anything {#step-3-measure-recallk-before-generating-anything}

For each question, is the supporting evidence in the top-k chunks that will
reach the generator? Do not stop at the gold document id: the needed passage
may sit in another chunk of the same document. Under the assumption of a
single, required, completely labelled piece of evidence, that rate is an upper
bound on evidence-grounded answers; nothing you do to the prompt reaches the
questions it misses. Decide in advance, from the cost of errors in your use
case, at what rate you stop and fix retrieval.

### Step 4 — generate, and log the context

Answer each question with the retrieved chunks in the prompt. For each answer,
log the query id, the model and prompt versions, the retrieved chunk ids, the
versions of the source documents and the generated answer. An answer without
its context is unattributable after the fact. If you work with real user data,
protect the logs according to your permission and retention policy, and do not
store personal data you do not need.

### Step 5 — attribute every failure

For each wrong answer, apply @sec-rag-failures's tests in order: first, did
evidence supporting the expected answer reach the generator; if so, are the
generated claims supported by it; if they are and the conclusion is still
wrong, mark source, label and synthesis causes separately. Produce a table of
counts.

### Step 6 — test the refusal

Run the unanswerable questions and count how many produced an ungrounded
answer anyway; on the answerable questions, report the unnecessary-abstention
rate separately. The two rates trade off against each other; plan a sufficient
sample for both and give them with confidence intervals.

### What to hand in

Evidence-chunk coverage and token cost for the two chunkings; an attribution
table for wrong answers that shows source/label uncertainty separately from
retrieval, grounding and synthesis; the ungrounded-answer and
unnecessary-refusal rates; and one paragraph naming the stage you would fix
first, why, and what it would cost.

## Exercises {#sec-rag-exercises}

1. **Reproduce the inversion.** Take 500 documents of your own and build two
   query sets — one asking what a document is about, one asking where a
   specific fact is. Sweep chunk size. Does the ranking invert on your corpus
   as it did on this one? If it does not, what is different about your
   documents?
2. **Measure evidence coverage.** Compute separately how often the *k*
   chunks your system actually passes to the model contain the needed
   evidence, and the end-to-end answer accuracy. Attribute the differences by
   hand on a sample to retrieval, parsing, source and generation faults; do not
   count the gap automatically as "generation's" or "retrieval's" problem —
   alternative answers, multiple pieces of evidence and the model's prior
   knowledge get in the way.
3. **Attribute a week of failures.** Take the wrong answers your system
   produced last week and sort them into missing evidence, unsupported claims,
   and source/label/synthesis. Report the proportions. Predict, before you
   look, which group will be largest.
4. **Test the parser.** Choose ten PDFs from your domain, extract the text and
   tables, and record in how many documents the row, column and header
   relations survived.
5. **Measure the amount of context.** Pass the top 1, 5, 10 and 20 chunks of
   the same fixed retrieval ranking to separate prompts; keep the chunk order
   and model settings fixed and compare evidence coverage and answer accuracy.
   Find the point, if there is one, where adding context starts to cost you
   [@shi2023large].
6. **Test the refusal.** Write twenty questions your corpus cannot answer.
   Count ungrounded answers, and unnecessary refusals on answerable questions.
   Then add an explicit abstention path and measure both again.
7. **Two granularities.** Index your corpus at both whole-document and
   sentence-packed granularity, route each query to one of them, and measure
   whether routing beats either index alone — the same question
   @sec-retrieval asked about retrievers, one level up.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-rag-deeper}

Before reading anything: inspect wrong answers sampled from your own system
across query types (fifty, say, recording the sampling period and the types)
and separate missing evidence, unsupported claims, wrong sources and
multi-evidence synthesis. The distribution can point you to the part of this
literature to start with.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [`ragas`](https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas) | an implementation of the two-halves evaluation; use it for the decomposition it forces, not the absolute numbers |
| [Eugene Yan on LLM patterns](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/) | an essay on LLM application patterns; compares RAG with the others by their trade-offs |
| [Chip Huyen's blog](https://huyenchip.com/blog/) | long-form applied writing on RAG and agent architectures |
| [`llama-index` documentation](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/) | library documentation; the ingestion and chunking sections |
| [Stanford CS224N](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) | lectures covering retrieval-augmented models and their evaluation |

## What to remember {#sec-rag-summary}

- **The needle test found nothing, and that is the chapter's first lesson.**
  Sixteen conditions, 640 queries, **100% at every context size and every
  position** up to 16,775 tokens — with 40 queries per cell, which is enough
  power to exclude a large positional collapse and not a small one.
  Lost-in-the-middle did not reproduce here because a verbatim string with a
  rare key is the easiest thing attention can do, not because the phenomenon is
  imaginary: @modarressi2025nolima removes the lexical overlap and watches
  eleven of thirteen long-context models fall below half their short-context
  baseline. A benchmark everything passes is not measuring your risk.
- **What survives is the cost, and it is large.** Eighty documents instead of
  the one that mattered: **148× the input tokens for identical accuracy**, paid
  on every request that cannot be served from a cache — prompt caching brings
  that nearer 15×, and only while the prefix is stable — with attention's
  quadratic share growing as the context does. Retrieval is not a crutch for a model that cannot read; it
  is how you stop paying for 79 documents you did not need.
- **Two reasons to retrieve are permanent and have nothing to do with window
  size.** The model is frozen and your documents are not, and a prompt cannot
  enforce who may see which document. A third is practical: most real corpora
  are far larger than any window.
- **Chunk size is a bet on the granularity of the question.** On one corpus,
  400-word chunks led article-level retrieval at **72.5%** recall@1 and came
  *last* on fact-level retrieval at **93.8%**; 50-word chunks did the reverse.
  The best configuration in one condition is the worst in the other, so a
  chunk size copied from a blog post is a guess about questions the author
  never saw.
- **Overlap is a repair, not a safety margin.** A 25-word overlap on 100-word
  chunks bought **+2.0 points** on fact-level queries and **−0.7** on
  article-level ones, for 29% more index. It fixes facts that straddle a
  boundary and nothing else.
- **Structure beat arithmetic, mostly.** Sentence-aligned chunks of ~100 words
  reached **97.8%** where fixed 100-word windows reached 95.5% — and matched the
  overlapping variant (97.5%, one query behind) with a **9% smaller** index. The sentence-aligned chunks
  are also smaller (86 words against 99); interpolating the fixed-size series
  credits roughly two of the 2.3 points to the boundary, but the size-matched
  control has not been run. The cheapest way to stop cutting through a
  fact is to cut where the text already breaks.
- **Watch the metric your consumer actually reads.** On fact-level queries,
  recall@1 moved four points across these configurations and recall@5 stayed
  between 97.2% and 100%; on article-level queries, recall@1 swung fifteen
  points and recall@5 still spanned ten. If your generator reads five chunks
  and your questions are fact-shaped, the chunking choice barely moves
  article retrieval; if it reads one, the R@1 columns *are* your system. Whether the retrieved chunk carries the answering sentence is a
  separate measurement, and this run does not make it.
- **Three failures, one symptom.** A wrong answer is a retrieval miss, a
  grounding miss, or a synthesis miss, and they have three different fixes.
  Attribute before you tune — the reflex fix, swapping the embedding model,
  addresses one of the three.
- **Number the chunks, ask for citations, and check them.** A citation is a
  claim too. Faithfulness (supported claims ÷ all claims) and context recall
  score the two halves over time, but they come from an LLM judge, so validate
  the judge before trusting the number.
- **A system with no way to abstain will not abstain.** Give it an explicit
  refusal output and then test it on questions the corpus cannot answer. That
  test is the one nobody runs, and it is the difference between a system that
  declines and one that has never been given the option.
